questions.question_text: Which unit is most suitable for the thickness of a credit card?

options.why: Centimetres are too large for such a thin object.
Metres are used for room-sized lengths, not card thickness.
Kilometres measure journeys, not tiny object thicknesses.

questions.solution_text: A credit card is about $1$ millimetre thick, so millimetres are most suitable.

questions.question_text: Which unit is most suitable for the length of a mobile phone?

options.why: Millimetres are unnecessarily small for the whole phone length.
A phone is much shorter than one metre.
Kilometres are used for long travel distances.

questions.solution_text: A phone is several centimetres long, so centimetres are suitable.

questions.question_text: Which unit is most suitable for the length of a tennis court?

options.why: Millimetres are far too small for a court length.
Centimetres are impractical for a court-sized length.
A tennis court is far shorter than a kilometre.

questions.solution_text: A tennis court is tens of metres long, so metres are suitable.

questions.question_text: Which unit is most suitable for the distance from Sydney to Canberra?

options.why: Metres are too small for a journey between cities.
Centimetres measure small objects, not intercity travel.
Millimetres are used for tiny lengths, not road distances.

questions.solution_text: Distances between cities are measured in kilometres.

questions.question_text: Which is the most sensible estimate for the height of a kitchen bench?

options.why: Nine millimetres is thinner than a finger, not bench height.
Nine metres is taller than a multi-storey building level.
Kilometres are completely unsuitable for furniture height.

questions.solution_text: A kitchen bench is just under $1$ metre high, so $90\text{ cm}$ is sensible.

questions.question_text: A student says a local walking trail is about $4\text{ m}$ long. What is the most likely correction?

options.why: Four millimetres is a tiny thickness, not a walking trail.
Four centimetres is shorter than a hand and cannot describe the trail.
Forty millimetres is still far too short for a walking trail.

questions.solution_text: A walking trail can sensibly be several kilometres long, so $4\text{ km}$ is the likely correction.
